metadata.title: Outlines
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: How a shader draws a line around a sprite
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation; Godot 4.7.2 on Apple M4 Pro (evidence/planning-checks); GPU Gems 2 chapter 34; see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Outlines. Learn how a shader draws a line around a sprite by asking each pixel about its neighbors, and the traps that make an outline vanish or break.

routing.reason: The lecture skill's approved first beat: portrait, title, narrated summary.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Most people picture an outline as a bigger copy of the sprite, hiding behind it. A shader has no second copy. Each pixel asks a question about its neighbors, and the answers draw the line.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. A texture is an image a shader can read. Alpha is how visible a pixel is. Opaque means fully visible. A neighbor is the pixel next to this one. And padding is empty space around an image.

terms.meaning: a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn
an image a shader can read by address
how visible a pixel is: 0 invisible, 1 solid
the pixel right next to this one
empty space added around an image

qc.sparse_reason: TERMS card: prerequisites, one plain line each.

beats.narration_text: A sprite can melt into a busy background. Watch what an outline does: one clean line around its shape, in any color you like. The picture file never changes. A shader draws the line.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Ask the Neighbors' (serif 40) top-left. A real Godot render in a framed window on the cream stage: the teal test sprite sits plain, then the outline shader switches on and a clean indigo line appears around its whole shape. Labels under the sprite: 'shader off', then 'shader on'.

beats.narration_text: The old trick draws a bigger copy of the sprite behind it. Scale a plus sign up a fifth: the tips get a thick border, the sides a thin one. Each edge moves in proportion to its distance from the middle.

shot.motion_claim: The copy swells out from behind the sprite: the border is fat at the tips and thin along the sides.

beats.narration_text: The shader asks something else. The graphics card runs one small program for every pixel, and each pixel checks its own alpha and the pixels around it. Am I empty, with an opaque neighbor? Then I am on the outline.

shot.visual_intent: A pixel grid (outline-only cells, no fill behind text) with the teal test sprite's silhouette as filled cells in the middle. One empty cell beside the sprite gets a terracotta ring and four short arrows to its four neighbors; the right neighbor is a filled cell and lights up. The ringed cell takes the line color (indigo) and a label reads 'on the outline'. Then a cell inside the sprite is asked: its own cell is opaque, label 'keeps its color', and it stays teal.

show.event: grid appears; a small program mark runs over every cell at once
one empty cell ringed, four arrows
the cell takes the line color

shot.motion_claim: A ring visits one empty cell, four arrows reach out, the right neighbor lights, the cell turns the line color; then a sprite cell is asked and keeps its color.

beats.narration_text: To look next door, a pixel reads the sprite's image at another address. The function is texture. U V is the pixel's own address, so U V plus a small step is the spot beside it.

shot.visual_intent: The series' uv_square: a square with a 0 to 1 axis across the top and down the left side (the second axis pointing DOWN). A terracotta dot rests at the middle with the glossary line 'UV: a point's address on the shape, 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down'. A second dot hops one small step to the right with a short arrow and the label 'UV + step'. A one-line code label 'texture(TEXTURE, UV + step)' types in under the square, with the glossary line 'TEXTURE: the node's own picture; texture(TEXTURE, uv) reads it' beside it.

show.event: square with axes, address dot at the middle
the dot hops right; code line types in

shot.motion_claim: The address dot hops one small step to the right, and the code line names exactly that hop.

beats.narration_text: What comes back is a color: four numbers, red, green, blue and alpha. Dot a picks the last one. Alpha zero is empty, alpha one is opaque. That one number is all the outline needs to know about a neighbor.

shot.visual_intent: One pixel's color drawn as four outline boxes in a row: r, g, b, a (monospace labels). The fourth box lifts out and drops onto a 0 to 1 scale with two marks: 0 'empty' (a swatch showing stage color through) and 1 'opaque' (a solid teal swatch). The code fragment '.a' is drawn beside the lifted box.

show.event: four boxes r g b a

shot.motion_claim: The fourth box lifts out of the row and lands on a 0 to 1 scale, once at 0 and once at 1.

lecture.runner_up: ClaudeCodeBeat with the line of code
lecture.why: Four numbers with the last one lifted out is the picture of '.a'.

beats.narration_text: Now the color. Mix blends two colors by an amount. Amount zero keeps the sprite's color, amount one gives the line color, and anything between is a blend. Outside zero to one, mix overshoots.

shot.visual_intent: The series' ramp strip as a color strip: the sprite's teal at the left end, the line indigo at the right end, end labels 0 and 1 and the glossary line 'mix(a, b, t): blends from a to b: t of 0 gives a, 1 gives b' above. A terracotta marker rides it to 0, then 0.5 (a blend), then 1. Then it continues past the right end to 2 and a small label 'overshoot' appears where the strip has ended.
shot.motion_claim: A marker rides a color strip from teal to indigo and then keeps going past the end of the strip.

lecture.why: A marker riding a strip is mix; overshoot is the marker leaving the strip.

beats.narration_text: First try, one question: is the pixel on my right opaque? If so, mix in the line color. Look what happens. Almost the whole sprite turns blue, because its own pixels have opaque neighbors too, and they all said yes.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the nine-line shader); at right a real Godot window: the plain sprite, then, as the voice says 'look what happens', the first try switches on and the whole sprite turns indigo except a thin teal crescent on its right edge.

show.event: the shader switches on, the sprite turns blue; readout 'all said yes'

cues.label: mix: blends from a to b by t

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · the shader on the left

shot.motion_claim: The around line is highlighted, then the COLOR line; then the plain sprite turns blue the moment the shader switches on.

beats.narration_text: So ask one more thing: am I empty? Multiply by one minus my own alpha. Opaque pixels have alpha one, so they get zero and keep their color. Only empty pixels, on the left of the sprite, stay blue.

shot.visual_intent: The same code card with the COLOR line highlighted and '* (1.0 - color.a)' marked; at right a real Godot window: the blue sprite of the first try, then, as the voice says 'multiply by one minus my own alpha', the fix switches on, the blue drains off and the sprite keeps its teal with only a thin indigo line along its left edge. One ring on the line, readout 'left side only'.

beats.narration_text: Now ask all four sides, and add the answers. Almost right, but the diagonal stretches come out lighter. There, two neighbors are opaque, the sum is two, and mix overshoots past the line color.

shot.visual_intent: Code card (the four reads added into one number, no cap); at right a real Godot window: the one-sided line of the last beat, then, as the voice says 'all four sides', a ring appears around the sprite, its diagonal stretches visibly lighter (periwinkle) than the rest. Two rings on the lighter stretches, readout 'sum = 2'.

beats.narration_text: Cap the sum with min. Min of the sum and one can never be more than one, so mix never overshoots. Now every pixel of the ring is the same blue. Four reads, one cap, one mix: a complete outline.

shot.visual_intent: The same code card with min(around, 1.0) marked; at right a real Godot window: the ring with lighter stretches, which settles, as the voice says 'so mix never overshoots', into a clean ring of one blue all the way round the sprite. Readout 'same blue'.

beats.narration_text: So far the step was point oh two: two percent of the picture. In pixels, that depends on the image: two and a half here, less than one on a thirty-two pixel sprite. Pixel art needs steps of whole pixels.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Pixel-Sized Steps' (serif 40) top-left. Three horizontal image strips stacked, drawn the same width and made of 32, 64 and 128 outline cells; on each a terracotta bracket spans two percent of the width and a grey label counts the cells it covers: 0.64, 1.28 and 2.56. The 128 strip's bracket covers two and a half cells; the 32 strip's covers less than one. Caption 'step 0.02'.
shot.motion_claim: A bracket of the same relative width settles on three strips and covers a different number of cells on each.

beats.narration_text: Another way to see it: each read is the whole picture, slid by the step. Four reads are four slid copies, added together. The outline is wherever the copies stick out past the sprite itself.

shot.visual_intent: The teal test circle drawn in the middle. Four ghost copies (grey circle outlines, each with a small terracotta dot at its center) slide out one step up, down, left and right and overlap. Where the ghosts stick out past the circle, the union is shaded in the line color: a ring. The original circle sits on top, teal, subtracting itself. Labels (1 to 3 words): 'read right', 'copy goes left', 'four copies', 'minus the sprite'.

show.event: the part past the sprite fills with the line color

shot.motion_claim: Four ghost copies slide out of the sprite, overlap, and the part that sticks out past the sprite fills with the line color.

beats.narration_text: The step counts pixels of the image, not of the screen. Draw the sprite twice as big, and thickness two becomes four screen pixels. Three times as big, six. The line grows with the sprite, which is what pixel art needs.

shot.visual_intent: One real sprite at three sizes in turn (drawn 1x, 2x, 3x) with the same thickness 2: the line around it is two, then four, then six canvas pixels wide. Readouts '2 px', '4 px', '6 px' under it.

beats.act: III · Say It with a Loop
beats.narration_text: Eight reads, written out: the four sides and the four corners. It works. It is also eight nearly identical reads, which is exactly where typos hide.

Code card at left: the eight-read shader (14 lines); the first two lines of reads are marked, then the two lines of corner reads, then all four read lines together. At right a real Godot window with the square sprite: with the four sides only, the corners of its line stay empty; as the voice says 'the four corners' they fill in and the frame is complete.

beats.act: III · Say It with a Loop
beats.narration_text: A loop says it once. For each y from minus one to one, and each x from minus one to one, read the alpha at that offset. Add it all up. Nine offsets, a three by three block.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left: the loop shader (14 lines); focus lands on the outer for, the inner for, the line that reads and adds, then the loop as a whole. At right the same complete frame on the square sprite, unchanged by rewriting the reads as a loop. A caption carries one plain line for 'for'.

cues.label: offset: an amount added to slide something

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · the shader on the left
props.caption: for: repeat a block once for each value in a range

shot.motion_claim: Focus steps into the loop: outer for, inner for, the read.

beats.act: III · Say It with a Loop
beats.narration_text: The block's middle is the pixel itself, an extra read that changes nothing on hard-edged art. And those float calls are not decoration: Godot refuses to build a vec two from two whole numbers. Here is its message.

shot.visual_intent: A 3 by 3 block of outline cells with offsets (-1,-1) to (1,1) written small in each cell and a terracotta center cell labelled 'me'. The nine cells light in loop order, row by row, and a '9 offsets' count ticks up. Beside it the one-line code 'vec2(float(x), float(y))' with the labels 'float: a decimal number' and 'vec2: a bundle of two numbers' on it, and under it a plain-shell box with the message the Shader Lab printed ('SHADER ERROR:' is the Lab's own prefix, the rest is the engine's text): SHADER ERROR: Invalid arguments for the built-in function: "vec2(int,int)".

show.event: block, nine cells light, middle marked

shot.motion_claim: The nine cells light one after another in loop order and the middle one is marked as the pixel itself.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. An outline is a question each pixel asks its neighbors. Steps count image pixels, from texture pixel size. A loop reads the neighbors, and the cost follows the reads. A shader paints only inside its rectangle, so pad the image. Thick lines bend the brush; thin parts and soft edges break it. Check padding, step size, reads, filter and modulate, yours or an AI's.
